tagline: A poem is language under pressure. Let a few words settle like indigo ink.

epigraph.text: Hope is the thing with feathers / That perches in the soul

art.note: The council decided the page should behave like a field notebook, with indigo ink settling for four seconds on rag and leaving a human trace rather than a responsive system.

writers.note: Field-notebook voice: indigo ink settles on rag, asking the reader to trace how pressure turns words into a poem.

nuggets.hook: A poem can make you smell rain without naming it.
nuggets.body: Look for the concrete noun doing the work: a leaf, a window, a stone. It can carry more than an adjective.

nuggets.hook: Break the line at the hinge and the poem turns.
nuggets.body: Line breaks decide when the reader pauses, so the same words can mean two different things. Try moving the break to the hinge.

nuggets.hook: Some words hum because their consonants knock.
nuggets.body: Say the line aloud and listen for hard stops, hisses, and repeating vowels. Sound can make meaning land before the brain catches up.

nuggets.hook: A sonnet can argue, confess, and turn in 14 lines.
nuggets.body: Form is a constraint that gives the poem a shape to push against. Find the turn - the place where the argument changes.
